beginner: Arugula likes loose, rich soil with plenty of compost that holds moisture but still drains well. It is not fussy and grows in most garden soils, but steady moisture keeps the leaves mild and tender; dry, hard soil makes them hot and tough and pushes the plant to flower.
seasoned: Arugula grows in a wide range of soils but does best in a fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam high in organic matter, kept evenly moist. As a fast leafy brassica it responds to compost worked in before sowing, which feeds quick growth and buffers the steady moisture that keeps the leaves tender and mild. It tolerates a fairly broad pH but leans toward 6.0 to 7.0, and keeping the soil out of the strongly acidic range also helps hold down clubroot, the brassica-family soil disease.

beginner: Arugula grows best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, about 6.0 to 7.0. A simple soil test tells you where you stand. Keeping the soil from getting too acidic also helps prevent clubroot, a cabbage-family soil disease.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0; arugula is forgiving and still does fine across roughly 5.5 to 7.5. Clemson lists 6.0 to 6.5 for the leafy greens in its arugula fact sheet. As with other brassicas, holding the soil toward neutral rather than strongly acidic also helps suppress clubroot, so a grower with clubroot history should lean to the high end.

beginner: Arugula grows fast and likes a little nitrogen for tender green leaves. Mix some compost or fertilizer into the soil before planting, then give it one light feeding a couple of weeks after the seeds come up. Because the crop is so quick, you usually do not need to feed it again.
seasoned: Arugula is a fast leafy brassica that runs on nitrogen, but the crop is so quick that one light feeding is usually plenty. Work compost or a balanced fertilizer in before sowing, then side-dress lightly with nitrogen about 2 to 3 weeks after the seedlings emerge to push tender, mild leaves. Avoid heavy nitrogen late, since lush growth draws aphids and flea beetles and does not improve a crop you will cut within a few weeks.

beginner: Time to give your arugula a light feeding.
seasoned: Time to side-dress your arugula with a little nitrogen.

beginner: Use a nitrogen-rich feed such as blood meal or a 21-0-0 fertilizer once, when the plants are a couple of weeks old.
seasoned: High N for fast leafy growth; a light side-dress of 21-0-0 or blood meal 2 to 3 weeks after emergence. No phosphorus or potassium needed beyond a soil-test baseline; do not overfeed a 3-to-4-week crop.

beginner: Follow the label rate for a nitrogen-rich vegetable fertilizer, one light feeding a few weeks after the seeds sprout.
seasoned: About a quarter cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row, side-dressed once a few weeks after emergence; for baby-leaf patches a single compost-rich bed often needs no extra feed at all.

beginner: Lots of tiny round shot holes peppering the leaves, made by tiny dark beetles that jump like fleas when you come near. Arugula is one of their favorites, and heavy damage can riddle or kill young seedlings.
seasoned: Small round shot-holes pepper the foliage and the tiny dark beetles jump when disturbed. Arugula and other mustards are highly preferred hosts, so pressure is often intense; seedlings can be stunted or killed and the holes mar the harvested leaves of a crop eaten raw.

beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew little pits and holes in cabbage-family leaves. They are drawn strongly to arugula and mustard and hit small seedlings hardest, since a tiny plant cannot outgrow the damage.
seasoned: Crucifer and striped flea beetles (Phyllotreta species) chew the foliage of brassicas and strongly prefer arugula and mustard; adults overwinter in debris and emerge to attack the earliest, smallest plants. Multiple generations occur through the season.

beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover from the day you sow, and if beetles are heavy use a spinosad spray or a kaolin clay coating. The main goal is to get the seedlings up and big fast, before the beetles riddle them.
seasoned: Floating row cover from sowing is the most effective tool; spinosad or kaolin clay help under heavy pressure. The aim is rapid establishment past the vulnerable seedling stage, so push fast growth.

beginner: Use row cover from sowing (the single best defense), keep seedlings growing fast with steady water, sow when beetles are less active, and clear nearby cabbage-family weeds. Some growers plant a sacrificial arugula patch as a trap crop.
seasoned: Exclude beetles with row cover from sowing, keep seedlings vigorous with even water and a light feed, clean up crucifer weeds and crop debris, and consider an early trap planting of arugula or mustard to divert beetles from the main crop.

beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or gray insects on the undersides of leaves and on new growth, sometimes with curled, sticky leaves. The waxy gray-green cabbage aphid hides deep in the crinkles and is hard to wash out.
seasoned: Colonies of green peach aphids and the waxy gray-green cabbage aphid (Brevicoryne brassicae) on leaf undersides and tips distort the foliage; honeydew and the aphids lodged in the leaves contaminate a raw-eaten crop, and several aphids vector viruses.

beginner: Aphids are small insects that suck sap from the plant. They breed quickly, especially on soft growth from too much fertilizer, and they can spread plant viruses; the cabbage aphid in particular loves brassicas like arugula.
seasoned: Several aphid species feed on arugula; they reproduce rapidly, favor the soft growth excess nitrogen produces, and the cabbage aphid is especially hard to dislodge from sheltered leaf folds.

beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap or neem oil, hitting the undersides of the leaves. Repeat every few days until they are gone, and pick before a colony lodges in the leaves.
seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong water jet or spray insecticidal soap or neem, covering leaf undersides; repeat every few days. Conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps.

beginner: Welcome helpful bugs like ladybugs and lacewings, go easy on nitrogen, check new growth often, and use row cover, which also keeps out flea beetles.
seasoned: Scout growing tips early, avoid overfeeding nitrogen, conserve natural enemies, and exclude with row cover; harvest the quick crop before colonies build.

beginner: Ragged chewed holes in the leaves, green caterpillars on the plants, and dark droppings. Because you eat the leaves, even a little chewing is a problem.
seasoned: Ragged feeding holes with green or striped larvae and frass; imported cabbageworm, cabbage looper, and diamondback moth larvae feed on arugula, and on a fast leaf crop even light feeding downgrades the harvest.

beginner: Several moths and white butterflies lay eggs on cabbage-family leaves, and the caterpillars that hatch (imported cabbageworms, loopers, and small wriggling diamondback larvae) chew the foliage.
seasoned: The larvae of several brassica moths and butterflies feed on the foliage; the adults lay eggs on the leaves, and warm-region plantings see the most pressure.

beginner: Spray Bt, which is safe and targets only caterpillars, or pick them and their eggs off by hand from the undersides of leaves. Spray again after rain, since it washes off.
seasoned: Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) or spinosad targeting young larvae and hand-pick where practical; repeat after rain.

beginner: Use a row cover to keep the adults from laying eggs, clean up old cabbage-family plants and weeds, and check leaf undersides for eggs and small caterpillars.
seasoned: Exclude egg-laying adults with row cover, clean up brassica debris and weed hosts, and scout leaf undersides for eggs and early instars.

beginner: Ragged holes with smooth edges chewed in low leaves, slimy trails on the leaves and soil, and worst damage in cool, damp, shady spots and after rain.
seasoned: Smooth-edged holes in low foliage with silvery slime trails, worst in cool, wet, densely planted or heavily mulched beds; a tender low salad green like arugula is highly susceptible.

beginner: Slugs and snails are soft, moisture-loving mollusks that feed at night and rasp holes in tender low greens like arugula. They thrive in damp mulch and dense, shaded plantings.
seasoned: Several slug and snail species feed nocturnally, rasping the foliage; they shelter in moist debris and mulch by day and build up in cool, wet conditions.

beginner: Hand-pick at night or after rain, set out shallow traps, and use an iron-phosphate slug bait, which is pet-safe. Reduce damp hiding places and water in the morning so the surface dries by night.
seasoned: Hand-pick after dark or rain, use shallow traps and iron-phosphate baits (pet-safe), and remove daytime shelter; morning watering lets the surface dry before they feed.

beginner: Thin and space plants for airflow, keep mulch light near the plants, clear damp debris, and water early in the day rather than at dusk.
seasoned: Reduce moisture and shelter near the plants: thin for airflow, keep mulch off the crowns, clear debris, and irrigate in the morning rather than the evening.

beginner: Pale yellow or angular patches on the tops of the leaves with a fuzzy grayish-white mold on the undersides, mostly in cool, damp, crowded conditions. Bad cases discolor and collapse the leaves.
seasoned: Angular yellow-to-brown lesions on the upper leaf surface with grayish-white sporulation beneath, spreading in cool, wet, humid weather; lesions brown and the leaves collapse. It is a leading arugula disease.

beginner: A mold-like disease that loves the same cool, wet weather arugula grows in, spreading through wet leaves and splashing water. Crowded plants and long leaf wetness make it worse.
seasoned: Hyaloperonospora parasitica (the brassica downy mildew oomycete), favored by cool temperatures, long leaf wetness, and high humidity; it spreads by wind- and splash-borne spores and survives on debris.

beginner: Remove the worst leaves, open up the airflow so leaves dry faster, and water at the soil instead of over the plants. It is hard to stop once it gets going, so prevention matters most.
seasoned: Cultural control dominates: improve airflow, avoid overhead irrigation, and remove infected leaves and debris; there is no rescue once it is established in humid weather.

beginner: Space plants for good airflow, water at the base, choose resistant varieties where available, and rotate where you plant arugula and other brassicas.
seasoned: Widen spacing for airflow, use drip rather than overhead water, choose resistant cultivars where offered, and rotate away from brassicas for several years.

beginner: White, blister-like bumps on the undersides of the leaves, with yellow spots on top. Badly spotted leaves are not good to eat.
seasoned: White, blister-like pustules on leaf undersides with chlorotic spotting above; severe infection distorts and downgrades the foliage. A common brassica-greens disease, worse in the South.

beginner: A different mold-like disease, not a true rust, that makes white pustules on cabbage-family leaves and spreads in cool, moist weather. It can ruin a leafy crop quickly.
seasoned: The oomycete Albugo candida, favored by cool nights, mild days, and leaf wetness; it spreads by splash- and wind-dispersed spores and survives on debris and as oospores.

beginner: Remove and destroy infected leaves, improve airflow, and water at the soil line. As with downy mildew, prevention works better than trying to cure it.
seasoned: Remove infected leaves and debris, improve airflow, and avoid overhead irrigation; chemical options are limited for the home garden.

beginner: Space plants out, avoid wetting the leaves, choose resistant varieties where it is common, and rotate your planting spot.
seasoned: Grow resistant cultivars where white rust is endemic, space for airflow, use drip irrigation, and rotate away from brassicas.

beginner: Seeds that never come up, or seedlings that flop over at the soil line with a pinched, rotted stem and then die. It strikes in cold, wet soil.
seasoned: Poor stands from seed and pre- or post-emergence collapse of seedlings with water-soaked, pinched stems at the soil line, worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil where germination is slow.

beginner: Soil fungi attack the seeds and tiny seedlings, especially when the soil is cold and soggy and the seeds are slow to come up.
seasoned: Soilborne Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium species attack germinating seed and seedlings; cold, saturated soil that slows emergence favors them.

beginner: There is no cure for an affected seedling, so focus on prevention. Pull and discard collapsed seedlings.
seasoned: No cure once seedlings collapse; manage by prevention and remove affected plants.

beginner: Do not sow into cold, soggy soil, plant shallowly in well-drained ground, do not overwater, and use fresh seed so it comes up fast.
seasoned: Sow shallowly into well-drained soil when temperatures favor quick emergence, avoid overwatering, and use fresh viable seed.

beginner: Small dark spots on the leaves that grow into round patches, sometimes with rings like a tiny target or a pale halo. Spotted leaves are not good to eat.
seasoned: Small dark lesions enlarge into circular spots, Alternaria often with concentric rings (a target look) and Cercospora as gray-brown spots with a halo; on a leaf crop even moderate spotting reduces the harvest. Favored by warm, wet conditions.

beginner: Fungi that spread in warm, wet weather and infect the leaves, leaving spots. They are worse on stressed plants and in crowded, damp plantings.
seasoned: Alternaria (A. brassicae, A. brassicicola) and Cercospora fungi infect brassica foliage, spreading by spores in wind and splashing water; infected seed, crop debris, and long leaf wetness drive them.

beginner: Remove and destroy spotted leaves, improve airflow so leaves dry quickly, and avoid wetting the leaves when you water. Start with clean seed.
seasoned: Remove spotted leaves and debris, improve airflow, and avoid overhead watering; a copper-based fungicide can help under heavy pressure.

beginner: Use clean seed, rotate away from brassicas, space plants for airflow, water at the soil line, and clear crop debris.
seasoned: Use clean, disease-free seed, rotate away from brassicas, space for airflow, water at the soil line, and clear crop debris that harbors spores.

beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 to 1.5 inches a week.
seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 inches per week, kept even; arugula is shallow-rooted and bolts faster and turns hotter under drought stress.

beginner: Aim for about 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week, a bit more when it is warm.
seasoned: Roughly 1 to 1.5 inches per week, more in warm, dry spells.

beginner: Water at the base of the plants rather than over the leaves, which helps prevent leaf diseases.
seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose; keeping the foliage dry checks downy mildew and white rust on a crop you eat raw.

beginner: Lower leaves yellow, seedlings rot at the base, and leaves get moldy in soggy, crowded beds.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, damping-off in seedlings, and downy mildew in crowded, constantly wet stands.

beginner: Wilting leaves that turn extra spicy and tough, and a plant that bolts (flowers) sooner than it should.
seasoned: Wilting, slowed growth, hotter and tougher leaves, and faster bolting; drought stress both sharpens the flavor and triggers the seedstalk.

beginner: Arugula sprouts quickly. Keep the top of the soil damp until it comes up.
seasoned: Arugula germinates fast; keep the shallow-sown seedbed evenly moist and uncrusted through emergence.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly damp, since the roots are shallow.
seasoned: Keep the seedlings evenly moist; arugula is shallow-rooted with little drought buffer.

beginner: Water evenly, about 1 to 1.5 inches a week, as the leaves grow.
seasoned: Keep even moisture through the few weeks of leaf growth at about 1 to 1.5 inches a week.

beginner: Keep the water steady while you pick leaves. If arugula dries out or the weather warms, it bolts and the leaves get much hotter and sharper, so steady watering keeps them mild.
seasoned: Steady moisture through leaf growth, and during any warm or lengthening-day spell, delays bolt and keeps the peppery bite mild; arugula turns hotter and harsher under drought stress. Cut young leaves and keep it watered for a milder, longer harvest.

beginner: Once arugula flowers the leaves get sharp and tough, and watering will not fix it (the flowers are edible, though). Resow when it is cooler for mild leaves.
seasoned: Once it bolts, the leaves sharpen and toughen and watering will not reverse it, though the flowers are edible. Resow in cooler conditions for mild leaves.

beginner: Keep the water steady so the leaves stay mild and tender and the plant does not bolt early.
seasoned: Even moisture keeps arugula growing fast, tender, and mild; dry, hot spells push it to flower and make the leaves harshly pungent.

seasoned: Steady moisture through the few weeks of leaf growth, and during any warm or lengthening-day spell, matters most for delaying bolt and keeping the bite mild.

beginner: Arugula is best planted straight in the garden from seed, because it grows so fast and does not like having its roots disturbed. Sow the seeds about a quarter to half an inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, since they sprout even in cold soil and the plants handle frost. Sow again every couple of weeks, and in hot areas plant in fall through spring instead of summer, because heat keeps the seeds from sprouting well and makes the plants bolt.
seasoned: Arugula is almost always direct-sown, since it grows fast and resents root disturbance. Sow seed about 0.25 to 0.5 inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring; it germinates readily even in cool soil, often in 5 to 7 days, and tolerates frost, so it can go in several weeks before the last frost. Sow a little more thickly than the final stand and thin to taste, eating the thinnings. In hot regions, shift sowing to fall through spring, since warm soil above about 80°F cuts germination and lengthening warm days bolt the crop.

beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
seasoned: A light, well-drained potting mix high in organic matter.

beginner: Mix in some compost for steady nutrients.
seasoned: Blend in compost and a little starter nitrogen; arugula is a quick feeder but needs only a light charge for its short life.

seasoned: Shallow containers dry faster than beds; check moisture daily in warmth and water before the mix dries, since drought stress bolts arugula and sharpens its flavor.

seasoned: Container arugula needs only a light starter feed; frequent watering leaches nutrients, but the crop is harvested before heavy feeding would matter.

beginner: In mild areas, a pot of fall-sown arugula can keep going through winter in a sheltered, sunny spot. In cold areas, move the pot against the house or into a cold frame, or cover it during hard freezes, and it will often resume in spring.
seasoned: Arugula is cold-hardy, so a fall-sown container can overwinter in mild zones, holding through winter in a sheltered spot and resuming in spring. In cold zones the limited root volume freezes harder than open ground, so sink the pot, move it to a cold frame or unheated structure, or cover it during hard freezes; an overwintered pot then yields the earliest spring picking.

beginner: Arugula is an easy, fast container crop. Use a wide, shallow pot at least 6 inches deep, sow the seed thickly, and snip baby leaves cut-and-come-again. Keep it watered and in the cool seasons, and give it some afternoon shade in warm weather to slow bolting.
seasoned: Arugula is one of the best container salad crops: shallow-rooted, fast, and happy sown densely for cut-and-come-again baby leaf in a broad container at least 6 inches deep. Keep moisture even, since shallow pots dry fast and drought triggers bolting, grow it in the cool seasons, and give afternoon shade in warm spells. A pot is also the easiest way to move the crop into shade or shelter as the weather turns.

seasoned: A self-watering container suits arugula well, since it smooths out the steady moisture that keeps the leaves mild and slow to bolt.

seasoned: Arugula is shallow-rooted, so depth matters less than surface area: a wide, shallow container at least 6 inches deep gives more sowing area for cut-and-come-again leaves and buffers the fast drying narrow pots suffer.

beginner: Other cabbage-family plants like broccoli, cabbage, kale, mustard, radishes, and arugula itself, because they share the same pests and diseases.
seasoned: Other brassicas: cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, collards, mustard, radish, turnip, and arugula itself. They share the cabbage-family pests (flea beetles, cabbage caterpillars, aphids) and the soilborne clubroot, so following one brassica with another concentrates and builds that pressure.

beginner: Try not to grow arugula or other cabbage-family plants (broccoli, kale, cabbage, mustard, radishes) in the same spot more than about once every 3 years. They share pests like flea beetles and a soil disease called clubroot that build up when these crops keep coming back. Plant arugula after peas, beans, onions, squash, or tomatoes instead.
seasoned: Rotate arugula and its brassica relatives so they do not return to the same ground for about 3 years. The cabbage-family pest complex (flea beetles above all, plus cabbage caterpillars and aphids) and the soilborne clubroot organism build up where brassicas repeat, and arugula's quick succession plantings make it easy to keep flea beetles cycling in one bed. Follow brassicas with legumes, alliums, cucurbits, or nightshades, and keep the soil near neutral to help suppress clubroot.

beginner: Arugula flowers (bolts) quickly when it gets warm and the days get long, and the leaves turn harshly spicy and bitter. To avoid it, grow arugula in the cool parts of the year, especially fall, sow a fresh little batch every 2 to 3 weeks, water steadily, and give it some afternoon shade when it is warm. Pick it promptly, and as soon as you see a flower stalk in the middle, harvest the whole plant.
seasoned: Arugula bolts fast once it is warm and the days lengthen, and the leaves turn sharply hot and bitter as it does. Keep the productive window in the cool shoulders of the year: sow early in spring and crop quickly, lean on the fall crop, choose slower-bolting types or wild (Diplotaxis) rocket where heat is a problem, give light afternoon shade in warm spells, and keep moisture steady. Succession sow every 2 to 3 weeks so a bolted batch is quickly replaced, and harvest promptly at the first sign of a central stalk.

beginner: Arugula bolts (sends up a flower stalk and turns very sharp and bitter) when it gets warm and the days are long. It happens fast and is just the plant's natural cycle, not a mistake. Grow it in cool weather, pick it young, and enjoy the flowers too, which are edible and peppery. Left alone, arugula often drops seed and comes up again on its own.
seasoned: Bolting in arugula is driven by heat and lengthening days, sped by drought and crowding, and it comes on fast because the plant is so quick. Once a central seedstalk rises the leaves narrow and flood with the mustard-oil compounds that make a sharp, almost acrid pungency, so the eating window closes quickly. The flowers are edible and peppery, and one plant left to bloom feeds pollinators and self-sows readily.

beginner: Do not leave arugula out on the counter. It wilts fast in the warmth, so get it into the fridge soon after picking.
seasoned: Arugula wilts and yellows within a day at room temperature, so refrigerate it promptly after cutting; if it must sit briefly, keep it cool and out of the sun.

beginner: Store arugula unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge crisper drawer, where it keeps about a week if kept very cold. Wash it only when you are ready to use it.
seasoned: Refrigerate unwashed in a loose or perforated bag in the crisper; arugula holds about 5 to 10 days near 32°F at high humidity. It is more perishable than sturdy greens like kale, so use it promptly, and wash only at use, since trapped moisture speeds breakdown.

beginner: Arugula is best fresh and does not freeze well for salads. If you have extra, turn it into pesto and freeze that, or blanch it briefly and freeze it to cook later.
seasoned: Arugula is a salad green and does not freeze well for raw use, losing its texture; if you have a glut, blanch briefly and freeze for cooking, or make pesto and freeze that, where its peppery bite holds up.

beginner: Arugula is best right after you pick it and does not keep long. Chill it quickly and use it within a week or so, and remember the flavor gets stronger the longer it sits.
seasoned: Quality is highest straight from the garden. Arugula is delicate and short-lived once cut, so chill it fast and use it within a week or so fresh; its peppery flavor also turns stronger and harsher in storage, another reason to eat it young and soon.

beginner: For a quick, peppery salad green, grow standard salad arugula like Roquette or the milder Astro, which are fast but flower quickly in heat. For hot weather or a longer-lasting patch, try wild arugula (sold as Sylvetta), which is slower to bolt, more intense in flavor, and can come back year after year in mild areas. Cut-leaf kinds like Surrey are great for snipping baby leaves again and again.
seasoned: Match the type to the slot. Standard salad rocket (Eruca sativa, Roquette and the like) is fastest and most pungent but bolts quickly in heat, so it suits the cool shoulders and baby-leaf cutting. Milder, broad-leaf selections like Astro give a gentler bite and quick baby leaf. For warm weather and a longer stand, wild or perennial rocket (Diplotaxis tenuifolia, sold as Sylvetta or wild arugula) is slower-growing, far slower to bolt, and more intensely flavored, and it can persist as a short-lived perennial in mild climates. Cut-leaf types like Surrey and Esmee are bred for tidy, regrowing baby-leaf patches.

beginner: Arugula is small, fast, and easygoing, so it tucks in between slower crops. It grows well next to lettuce and other quick greens, bush beans, and aromatic herbs like dill, and alliums such as onions. The main thing is to keep it away from other cabbage-family plants, which share its pests and diseases, and to watch for flea beetles, which love it.
seasoned: Most arugula companion pairings rest on space, timing, and tradition rather than measured effects. The practical ones are structural: arugula is quick and shallow-rooted, so it interplants with lettuce and other fast greens and tucks beside legumes and aromatic herbs. Aromatic herbs and alliums are the traditional scent-based deterrents for the cabbage-family pests arugula shares. The well-grounded caution is to separate arugula from other brassicas, which share clubroot and the whole cole-crop pest complex, a rotation and disease principle more than a tested adjacency effect; arugula is also a flea-beetle magnet, sometimes deliberately used as a trap crop near choicer brassicas.

beginner: Beans add a little nitrogen to the soil that the leafy arugula can use, and the two share a cool-to-mild season without competing much.
seasoned: A legume interplant on nitrogen and structure: beans fix a little nitrogen the leafy arugula draws on, and the quick arugula uses the ground between young bean plants. Sound space and timing logic rather than a measured arugula effect.

beginner: Lettuce grows fast and low like arugula, so you can sow them together to fill a salad bed, and both like the same cool weather.
seasoned: Arugula and lettuce share a cool season, a shallow root zone, and a salad bed, so they interplant efficiently and are cut young together. A space-and-timing pairing, not a documented growth boost; the two share no major pest.

beginner: Strong-smelling herbs like dill are a classic neighbor for cabbage-family plants; their scent is said to confuse pests, and their flowers bring in helpful insects.
seasoned: Aromatic umbels like dill draw the parasitoid wasps and predators that attack brassica aphids and caterpillars, and extension work pairing umbels with cole crops has shown reduced damage. Let some flower nearby; a partial-mechanism aid, not a measured arugula-specific effect.

beginner: Onions are a traditional neighbor for cabbage-family plants; their strong smell is thought to help put off the pests that hunt by scent.
seasoned: Alliums are the classic scent-based brassica companion, their pungency thought to mask the crop from cabbage pests that locate hosts partly by smell. Shallow-rooted and undemanding, they tuck around arugula without competing. Traditional with partial mechanistic support, not an arugula-specific measured effect.

beginner: Keep arugula away from other cabbage-family plants like broccoli, cabbage, kale, mustard, and radishes. They share the same pests and diseases, so planting them together makes flea beetles and clubroot worse.
seasoned: Planting arugula shoulder to shoulder with its brassica relatives, broccoli, cabbage, kale, mustard, radish, concentrates the shared cabbage-family pests, flea beetles above all, plus cabbage caterpillars and aphids, and repeated same-family planting builds soilborne clubroot. Spread brassicas out and rotate where they grow. Because arugula is a strong flea-beetle draw, some growers exploit this and use it as a sacrificial trap crop away from choicer brassicas.

beginner: The first pair of little rounded leaves poking up. Arugula sprouts fast, often in under a week, even in cool soil.
seasoned: The first pair of rounded seed leaves pushing up through the soil. Arugula comes up fast, often in 3 to 7 days, even in cool soil, and germination is usually even if the surface has not dried out.

beginner: Keep the soil surface evenly moist but not soggy until the seedlings are up. Arugula sprouts well in cool soil but badly in hot soil, so sow in spring or fall, not the heat of summer.
seasoned: Keep the soil surface consistently moist but never waterlogged until seedlings are up. Arugula germinates well in cool soil but poorly in warm soil above about 80°F, so early-spring and fall sowings come up best.

beginner: Any sprouts yet?
seasoned: Any sprouts yet?

beginner: The first true leaves, which look like tiny versions of the grown arugula leaf. Now you can thin them.
seasoned: The first true leaves, lobed little versions of the grown leaf. Now you can tell seedlings from weeds and start thinning.

beginner: Arugula is a fast-growing, cool-season salad green with a peppery, mustardy flavor. It is one of the quickest things you can grow, giving baby leaves in about 3 weeks, and it handles frost and even grows through winter in mild areas. Its main quirk is that it bolts (sends up a flower stalk) very fast in heat and long days, and the leaves turn sharply hot and bitter when it does. So it grows best in the cool parts of the year, especially fall, and in hot places it is a fall-to-spring crop. Sow a little every couple of weeks for a steady supply. It is easy and beginner-friendly; the main pest to watch is the flea beetle, which chews tiny holes in the leaves. There is also a wild kind of arugula that is slower to bolt and even more peppery.
seasoned: Arugula (Eruca sativa), also called salad rocket or roquette, is a fast, cool-season leafy green in the mustard family (Brassicaceae), grown for its tender, peppery leaves. It is one of the quickest crops in the garden, giving baby leaves in about 3 weeks and full leaves in around a month, and it germinates readily even in cool soil and tolerates frost, so it can be sown very early and overwinters in mild zones. Its defining habit is how fast it bolts: heat above about 75°F and lengthening days send it to seed quickly, and the leaves turn sharply hot and bitter as it does, so the spring window is short, fall is the main crop, and in hot regions it is grown through the cool fall, winter, and spring. A separate wild or perennial rocket (Diplotaxis tenuifolia, sold as Sylvetta) is slower, more pungent, and far slower to bolt. Arugula is easy, succession-sown every 2 to 3 weeks, and a strong first-season choice, though flea beetles are its signature pest.

beginner: Arugula is ready to pick as soon as the leaves are big enough, often baby leaves in about 3 weeks and full leaves in around a month. Take the outer leaves a few at a time, or cut the whole patch about an inch above the soil so it grows back. seasoned: Arugula is ready as soon as the leaves are big enough to use, often baby leaf at 2 to 3 weeks and full leaf around 30 to 40 days. Cut the outer leaves cut-and-come-again, or shear the whole patch about an inch above the crown and let it regrow for a second or third cutting. Pick young and in the cool morning, and crop fast as the weather warms, since the leaves turn sharply hot and bitter once the plant bolts.

beginner: Arugula is usually sown a bit thick, then thinned. For baby leaves you can leave it dense, about an inch or two apart; for bigger plants, thin to 4 to 6 inches. Do not waste the thinnings, they are tender baby arugula.
seasoned: Sow a little thick and thin in stages: for baby-leaf cutting, leave plants dense at 1 to 3 inches; for larger, full plants, thin to 4 to 6 inches. Eat every thinning as tender baby arugula, so thinning is just an early harvest. Crowded plants compete, stay small, and bolt sooner.
